back: **Internal** economies lower costs when the **business grows**; **external** economies lower costs when the **whole market/industry grows**.

front: Define **purchasing economies of scale**.
back: **Purchasing economies** occur when large firms **buy in bulk** and receive **discounts**, lowering the average cost per unit.

front: What are managerial economies of scale?
back: When large firms can afford **specialist, highly skilled managers**, whose greater efficiency **lowers average costs**.

front: Name two internal economies of scale.
back: **Purchasing** economies and **managerial** economies.

front: Name two external economies of scale.
back: A **better-skilled workforce** and **improved infrastructure**.

front: How does a better-skilled workforce create external economies of scale?
back: A growing industry concentrates **skilled workers** who need **less training** and become **productive quickly**, lowering costs.

front: Improved transport and communications <u>  </u> in a growing industry can make distribution more efficient.
back: Improved transport and communications **infrastructure** in a growing industry can make distribution more efficient.

front: Economies of scale help large firms lower their costs of production beyond what <u>  </u> firms can achieve.
back: Economies of scale help large firms lower their costs of production beyond what **small** firms can achieve.

front:
**True or False?**

Bulk-buying raw materials is an example of a purchasing economy of scale.
back:
**True.**

Buying in **greater volume** earns **bulk discounts**, reducing the **cost per unit**.

front: What happens to average costs once a firm grows beyond its minimum-cost level of output?
back: They **start to rise again** as **diseconomies of scale** occur.

front: Define **diseconomies of scale**.
back: **Diseconomies of scale** are the reasons a firm's **average costs rise** as it grows **too large**.

front: What happens to average costs when a firm grows beyond its optimal size?
back: **Average costs start to rise** because of **diseconomies of scale**.

front: Name three causes of diseconomies of scale.
back: **Poor communication and coordination**, **increased bureaucracy**, and a **lack of commitment from employees**.

front: How does poor communication cause diseconomies of scale?
back: As a firm grows, the **chain of command lengthens**, so communication becomes **slower** and mistakes worsen efficiency, raising costs.

front: How does increased bureaucracy cause diseconomies of scale?
back: Larger firms are **more complicated to run**, needing extensive **administration**, staff and resources that raise average costs.

front: Why might employees become less committed as a business grows?
back: They may feel **less valued** with limited management contact, becoming **demotivated**, which lowers output and raises average costs.

front: The point at which a firm can no longer reduce its costs any further is called productive <u>  </u>.
back: The point at which a firm can no longer reduce its costs any further is called productive **efficiency**.

front: Many very large businesses break themselves into smaller autonomous <u>  </u> to communicate more effectively.
back: Many very large businesses break themselves into smaller autonomous **units** to communicate more effectively.

front:
**True or False?**

Diseconomies of scale mean a business can become so large that it becomes less efficient.
back:
**True.**

Beyond a certain size, problems such as poor communication make a business **less and less efficient**.

front:
**True or False?**

Diseconomies of scale cause average costs to fall.
back:
**False.**

Diseconomies of scale cause average costs to **rise** as the firm becomes too large.

front: How might a business reduce diseconomies of scale?
back: By **reconsidering its organisational structure** — e.g. breaking into **smaller autonomous units** to improve communication.

front: Name the three main methods of production.
back: **Job**, **batch**, and **flow (mass)** production.

front: Name two factors that affect the method of production a business chooses.
back: The **level of output**, the **nature** of the product, whether it is **standardised or customised**, and the **level of automation** (any two).

front: Define **job production**.
back: **Job production** is where products are made **individually** to meet the **specific requirements of individual customers**.

front: Give one advantage of job production.
back: **High customisation** and **attention to detail**, allowing a **premium price** and building **customer loyalty**.

front: Give one disadvantage of job production.
back: It is **expensive**, has **long lead times**, and its low volume prevents **economies of scale**.

front: Give an example of job production.
back: **Made-to-order furniture**, **tailored clothing** (suits, wedding dresses), or **bespoke jewellery**.

front: Define **batch production**.
back: **Batch production** is where products are made in **groups (batches)**, each batch completing the whole process before the next begins.

front: Give one advantage of batch production.
back: It can **switch between products** for different needs, is more **cost-effective** than flow for small quantities, and gains some **purchasing economies**.

front: Give one disadvantage of batch production.
back: **Set-up time between batches** causes down time, and **stock accumulates**, needing storage.

front: Batch production strikes a balance between customisation and <u>  </u>-effectiveness.
back: Batch production strikes a balance between customisation and **cost**-effectiveness.

front: Define **flow (mass) production**.
back: **Flow production** makes a product in a **continuous sequence of operations on a production line**, used for **high volumes of standardised products**.

front: Give one advantage of flow production.
back: It **minimises set-up/idle time**, gives **consistent quality**, uses **fewer skilled workers**, and has **short lead times**.

front: Give one disadvantage of flow production.
back: **High capital investment**, a **breakdown can halt the whole line**, and it does **not allow customisation**.

front: Flow production is commonly used for high volumes of <u>  </u> products, such as cars and electronics.
back: Flow production is commonly used for high volumes of **standardised** products, such as cars and electronics.

front:
**True or False?**

Job production is well suited to producing large quantities of identical products.
back:
**False.**

**Job** production is for **unique, low-volume** products; **flow** production suits large quantities of identical goods.

front:
**True or False?**

In batch production, each batch completes the whole production process before the next begins.
back:
**True.**

Each batch goes through the **entire production process** before the next batch starts.

front: Define **labour-intensive production**.
back: **Labour-intensive production** predominantly uses **physical labour** (rather than machinery) to produce goods or services.

front: Define **capital-intensive production**.
back: **Capital-intensive production** predominantly uses **machinery and technology** (rather than labour) to produce goods or services.

front: Where is labour-intensive production common?
back: In countries with **low labour costs** (e.g. Bangladesh), in **small-scale** production, and in **service delivery**.

front: Where is capital-intensive production common?
back: In **large-scale** production of **standardised products**, and in **developed countries** where **labour costs are high**.

front: Give one advantage of capital-intensive production.
back: **Low-cost production at high output**, **consistent and precise** machines that can **run without breaks**.

front: Give one disadvantage of capital-intensive production.
back: High **set-up and maintenance costs**, **breakdowns** can delay production, and **limited flexibility**.

front: Give one advantage of labour-intensive production.
back: **Low cost where labour is cheap**, workers can be **creative**, and they are **flexible** (they can be retrained).

front: Give one disadvantage of labour-intensive production.
back: Workers **may be unreliable** and need breaks, **incentives** may be needed to motivate them, and **training costs** can be significant.

front: Manufacturing in developed countries, where labour costs are relatively <u>  </u>, is likely to be capital-intensive.
back: Manufacturing in developed countries, where labour costs are relatively **high**, is likely to be capital-intensive.

front: Small-<u>  </u> production is likely to be labour-intensive.
back: Small-**scale** production is likely to be labour-intensive.

front:
**True or False?**

Capital-intensive production is best suited to small-scale, customised output.
back:
**False.**

Capital-intensive production suits **large-scale, standardised** output; **labour-intensive** production suits small-scale.

front:
**True or False?**

The delivery of services is usually more labour-intensive than manufacturing.
back:
**True.**

Services such as teaching rely heavily on **physical labour**, making them more labour-intensive than manufacturing.

front: Define **productivity**.
back: **Productivity** is the **output per worker** over a given time period.

front: What is the formula for productivity?
back: **Productivity = total output ÷ number of workers**.

front: A business produces 46,000 units with 50 workers. What is productivity per worker?
back: 46,000 ÷ 50 = **920 units per worker**.

front: Output is 69,000 units with 60 workers. What is productivity per worker?
back: 69,000 ÷ 60 = **1,150 units per worker**.

front: Productivity rises from 920 to 1,150 units per worker. What is the percentage change?
Name two ways a business can increase productivity.
back: **Motivating employees**, **training staff**, better **working practices**, and **investing in capital equipment** (any two).

front: The higher the level of productivity, the <u>  </u> the average total costs.
back: The higher the level of productivity, the **lower** the average total costs.

front: How can motivating employees increase productivity?
back: Motivated workers are **more productive** — e.g. **financial incentives linked to output**, or involving them in **decision-making**.

front: How does higher productivity make a business more competitive?
back: It **lowers average costs**, so the business can **cut prices** or make **higher profit**, and reinvest in further improvements.

front: How do customers benefit from higher productivity?
back: **Lower prices** (from reduced costs) and often better **quality and customer service**.

front: Workers may be rewarded for higher output with a <u>  </u> linked to their productivity.
back: Workers may be rewarded for higher output with a **bonus** linked to their productivity.

front:
**True or False?**

Higher productivity can create difficulties for workers, such as job losses or feeling overworked.
back:
**True.**

New machinery may cause **job losses**, and staff may feel **pressured** to increase output.

front:
**True or False?**

Productivity measures the total output of a business, regardless of the number of workers.
back:
**False.**

Productivity is **output per worker** — total output **divided by the number of workers**.

front: How can investment in capital equipment raise productivity?
back: **Automation** improves output and quality, makes **fewer mistakes**, and can run for **long periods without a break**.

front: Define **lean production**.
back: **Lean production** involves **minimising the resources** used in production, with a focus on **reducing waste**.

front: Give one benefit of lean production.
back: **Lower unit costs** (so lower prices), **higher quality** output, and **increased profit margins**.

front: Name two strategies used in lean production.
back: **Just-in-time (JIT) stock control** and **Kaizen**.

front: Define **just-in-time (JIT) stock management**.
back: **JIT** is where raw materials are **not stored onsite** but ordered and delivered by suppliers **just in time for production**.

front: What must a business have in place for JIT to work?
back: **Close relationships** with a **small number of trusted, reliable suppliers**, often in **close proximity**.

front: Give one advantage of JIT stock management.
back: **Lower storage/stockholding costs**, **improved cash flow**, and **free storage space** for productive use.

front: Give one disadvantage of JIT stock management.
back: No **bulk-buying economies**, **can't meet sudden demand rises**, and **unreliable suppliers can halt production**.

front: Define **Kaizen**.
back: **Kaizen** is **continuous improvement** — small, ongoing changes that **eliminate waste** and raise productivity.

front: How is Kaizen different from one-off improvements?
back: Kaizen makes **small, ongoing** changes that are **constantly reviewed**, rather than large one-off changes.

front: Kaizen requires all workers to be actively involved in making improvements, not just <u>  </u>.
back: Kaizen requires all workers to be actively involved in making improvements, not just **management**.

front: What does 'the seven wastes' refer to in lean production?
back: Seven types of waste minimised in lean production: **transportation, inventory, motion, waiting, overproduction, overprocessing and defects**.

front: Give two of the seven wastes in lean production.
back: **Transportation**, **inventory**, **motion**, **waiting**, **overproduction**, **overprocessing**, and **defects** (any two).

front: In lean production, <u>  </u> refers to anything that prevents a business from being efficient.
back: In lean production, **waste** refers to anything that prevents a business from being efficient.

front:
**True or False?**

Just-in-time production requires large amounts of stock to be held onsite.
back:
**False.**

**JIT** holds **minimal stock** — materials are delivered **just in time**, not stored onsite.

front:
**True or False?**

Kaizen relies on large, one-off changes to boost productivity.
back:
**False.**

Kaizen uses **small, continuous** improvements, not large one-off changes.

front: Give one benefit of reducing waste in production.
back: **Lower costs** and greater **competitiveness**, **better customer service**, and **environmental benefits**.

front: JIT is particularly useful for businesses in <u>  </u> markets, where products need frequent design changes.
back: JIT is particularly useful for businesses in **dynamic** markets, where products need frequent design changes.

front: What are robots used for in production?
back: To **automate production processes** — they use **sensors and AI** to collect information and improve performance.

front: Give two business uses of robots.
back: **Manufacturing/assembly**, **warehousing/logistics**, **agriculture**, **medicine/surgery**, and **hazardous testing** (any two).

front: Define **computer-aided design (CAD)**.
back: **CAD** is the process of **digitally creating design simulations** of products in 2D or 3D.

front: Define **computer-aided manufacturing (CAM)**.
back: **CAM** is the use of **computers to assist in manufacturing operations** such as production, planning and storage.

front: What is a drone, and how is it used in business?
back: An **unpiloted aircraft** used for tasks like **package delivery**, **photography**, and **crop monitoring/spraying**.

front: Give two advantages of using robots.
back: Increased **productivity** (no breaks/fatigue), improved **accuracy**, safer **hazardous tasks**, and lower **labour costs** in the long run.

front: Give two disadvantages of using robots.
back: **High initial investment**, **maintenance costs**, **lack of flexibility**, and possible **job losses**.

front: Robots can work continuously without breaks or <u>  </u>, which increases productivity.
back: Robots can work continuously without breaks or **fatigue**, which increases productivity.

front: What does 'flexibility' in production mean?
back: How easily a business can **switch to different machinery** to make different products (known as **retooling**).

front: Automation usually works best in the manufacture of <u>  </u> products.
back: Automation usually works best in the manufacture of **standardised** products.

front:
**True or False?**

Introducing technology in production is usually cheap and requires little training.
back:
**False.**

Installing technology has **significant costs**, needs **staff training**, and causes **down time** during installation.

front:
**True or False?**

Robots can perform dangerous tasks, improving workplace safety.
back:
**True.**

Robots can carry out **hazardous tasks** that are dangerous for humans, improving **safety**.

front: What is computer-integrated manufacturing (CIM)?
back: The **complete automation** of a manufacturing plant, with all processes functioning under **computer control**.

front: The most flexible production technology is also likely to be the most <u>  </u>.
back: The most flexible production technology is also likely to be the most **costly**.

front: Define the **factors of production**.
back: The **factors of production** are the **resources used to produce goods and services**.

front: Name the four factors of production.
back: **Land**, **labour**, **capital**, and **enterprise**.

front: Define **land** as a factor of production.
back: **Land** is the **non-man-made natural resources** available for production.

front: Define **capital** as a factor of production.
back: **Capital** is any **man-made resource** used to produce goods or services (e.g. tools, machines, buildings).

front: Define **labour** as a factor of production.
back: **Labour** is the **human input** into production — mental or physical effort, which can be **skilled or unskilled**.

front: Define **enterprise** as a factor of production.
back: **Enterprise** involves **taking risks** to set up or run a firm, combining the other factors to produce goods/services for **profit**.

front: Producing any good or service requires a combination of <u>  </u> four factors of production.
back: Producing any good or service requires a combination of **all** four factors of production.

front: Give an example of land as a factor of production.
back: **Natural resources** such as oil — e.g. **Kuwait** specialises in oil, which makes up 95% of its exports.

front: What does an entrepreneur do?
back: Decides the **combination of factors of production** needed to produce goods/services, aiming to **make a profit**.

front: In a capital-intensive process, what is labour mainly used for?
back: For **specialist-skill tasks** (e.g. design) and to **oversee the operation of machinery**.

front: Rapid advances in <u>  </u> have made capital-intensive processes more affordable for smaller businesses.
back: Rapid advances in **technology** have made capital-intensive processes more affordable for smaller businesses.

front: Why is winemaking (viticulture) a labour-intensive process?
back: It relies heavily on **workers** (pickers, viticulturists), with machinery used only for **hazardous or continuous** tasks like fermentation.

front:
**True or False?**

Only one or two factors of production are needed to make any good or service.
back:
**False.**

Producing any good or service needs a **combination of all four** factors of production.

front:
**True or False?**

In countries with low labour costs, such as Thailand and Vietnam, clothing is often mass-produced using labour-intensive processes.
back:
**True.**

Where **labour costs are low**, there is little incentive to use machinery, so production stays **labour-intensive**.

front: What is meant by 'quality'?
back: **Quality** is the **features of a product that satisfy the needs of customers**.

front: Give two things that make customers see a product as good quality.
back: It **looks good / has a reputable brand**, is **reliable and durable**, is **safe and fit for purpose**, and has **good customer service** (any two).

front: How can good quality give a business a competitive advantage?
back: It **attracts and retains loyal customers**, **lowers costs** (fewer defects and returns), and **builds reputation** as a USP.

front: What are the risks if a business does not maintain quality?
back: **Losing customers** to rivals, **higher costs** replacing faulty goods, and a **poor reputation** from bad reviews.

front: High quality with minimal defects lowers costs, allowing a business to charge lower selling <u>  </u> to compete.
back: High quality with minimal defects lowers costs, allowing a business to charge lower selling **prices** to compete.

front: Define **quality control**.
back: **Quality control** checks quality at the **end of the production process**, using **quality inspectors** to find faults.

front: Define **total quality management (TQM)**.
back: **TQM** is a **whole-business approach** to quality that aims to **eliminate problems before they occur**, involving **all employees**.

front: Give one advantage of quality control.
back: **Specialists check standards**, output is likely to be **fit for purpose**, and **little staff training** is needed.

front: Give one disadvantage of quality control.
back: Rejected goods **waste resources**, the **cause of defects is ignored**, and **scrapping or reworking is costly**.

front: Name two features of total quality management (TQM).
back: **Teamwork**, **zero defects** ('get it right first time'), **ongoing monitoring**, a focus on **customer needs**, and **committed, trained workers** (any two).

front: TQM aims for zero defects — a culture of getting it right first <u>  </u>.
back: TQM aims for zero defects — a culture of getting it right first **time**.

front:
**True or False?**

In quality control, faults are checked at the end of the production process.
back:
**True.**

Quality control uses **inspectors** to check for faults at the **end** of production.

front:
**True or False?**

In TQM, only the quality-control department is responsible for quality.
back:
**False.**

In **TQM**, **all employees** are responsible for quality in **every** business process.

front:
**True or False?**

Better quality reduces wastage and returns from unsatisfied customers.
back:
**True.**

Fewer defects mean **less wastage** and **fewer returns**, which lowers costs.
